SOURCE: "AlphaEval: Evaluating Agents in Production", Pengrui Lu*, Bingyu Xu*, Wenjun Zhang*, Shengjia Hua* (equal contribution) and 20+ co-authors, corresponding author Pengfei Liu. Affiliations: SII, MiraclePlus, SJTU, GAIR, HIT, UCAS, LangCore, Jiqizhixin, HunterAI, CinoCore, KuaFuAI, POET. Header "SII-GAIR". arXiv:2604.12162v1 [cs.CL], 14 Apr 2026. Preprint, no venue. Code: github.com/GAIR-NLP/AlphaEval.

COVERAGE: All 108,468 chars of the pypdf extraction were read. That covers the body, appendices A-J (including Table 10, the sensitivity analysis, the H.1/H.2 error analysis and the survey) and the reference list, which I only skimmed. I skimmed the Table 1 rows (90+ benchmark comparison) and the H.1 Mode D/E and H.2.1 text, whose output was cut off in my reading. I did not run the figures script.

NOTE FIT: I read the note's headings and grep hits, not the whole file (about 515 lines). It already uses "harness is a component too" evidence: Terminal-Bench, SWE-EVO, MLE-bench, AutoLab, DataSpace. The best-fit section is therefore "Evaluate the components, then the whole". The paragraph at line 255 ("The harness is a component too, so report model and harness together") is the right anchor. A secondary fit is "Agent-specific suites", beside the DataSpace/MerchantBench production-style paragraph at line 399. AlphaEval is not cited anywhere in the note. The ledger row says status "downloaded" and points at this note. No other note fits better. 05-llm-as-judge or 15-calibration-against-human-labels could take the judge-agreement numbers as a small sharpens. The note lacks these AlphaEval-specific points:
- A multi-paradigm grader mix per task, with expert-weighted composition.
- Dollar-value weighting.
- A practitioner survey.
- The production failure modes: infeasibility fabrication, format compliance, cross-section inconsistency.

CORE CLAIM: Research agent benchmarks are retrospectively curated and well-specified. AlphaEval instead builds 94 tasks from 7 companies that deploy agents commercially, across 6 O*NET domains. It scores whole agent products (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor), not bare models. The best product scores 64.41/100, and scaffold choice moves the score as much as model choice.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Best configuration is low.
 number: 64.41/100 (Claude Code + Opus 4.6).
 setup: 94 tasks, 14 model-scaffold configs, default API settings. Single run per config except the best, which has 3 runs. Judge in the LLM-judged parts is Claude Opus 4.6.
 quote: "the best configuration (Claude Code + Opus 4.6) achieves only 64.41/100, revealing a substantial research-production gap"
 where: Intro, p.2; Table 3, p.9.
2. Scaffold moves the same model.
 number: Opus 4.6 gets 64.41 (Claude Code), 61.85 (Cursor), 61.31 (Copilot), 53.45 (Codex). GPT-5.2 gets 39.47 (Claude Code) vs 54.91 (Copilot).
 setup: single run each; Codex used version 0.111.0 for GPT-5.2/Opus and 0.80.0 for GLM-5/Kimi (Table 6). The Opus comparison is the clean one.
 quote: "The same Claude Opus 4.6 scores 64.41 via Claude Code, 61.85 via Cursor, 61.31 via GitHub Copilot, but only 53.45 via Codex. GPT-5.2 scores 39.47 via Claude Code but 54.91 via GitHub Copilot—a 15-point spread."
 where: Sec 5.2, p.9.
3. Domain variance. Rankings flip by domain.
 number: P&O ranges 30.91 to 88.09; HR max 38.91; GLM-5 scores 66.43 on P&O but 52.46 on SE.
 quote: "Procurement & Operations scores range from 30.91 to 88.09, while Human Resources scores never exceed 38.91"
 where: p.9. Domain means: TR 62.0, P&O 61.7, SE 56.3, F&I 55.8, H&LS 38.6, HR 30.0. I recomputed TR and HR from Table 3 and they match.
4. Run-to-run stability, best config only.
 number: overall 64.41, CI [62.58, 66.24]. P&O std 4.72, F&I 1.87, TR 3.56.
 setup: 3 independent runs, Claude Code + Opus 4.6 only.
 quote: "The narrow confidence intervals (overall ±1.83) confirm that reported scores are stable and that configuration rankings are reproducible across runs."
 where: Sec 5.3, Table 4, p.10.
5. The LLM judge agrees with human experts about as well as they agree with each other.
 number: A vs B 84.7% agreement (κ 0.691); A vs judge 85.0% (κ 0.697); B vs judge 89.7% (κ 0.780); Fleiss κ 0.720.
 setup: 20 random LLM-judged tasks, 5 configs, 1,000 rubric-point judgments. Annotator A strict, B lenient. Judge is Opus 4.6.
 quote: "The automated judge shows higher agreement with the lenient annotator (κ= 0.780) than the strict one (κ= 0.697), consistent with known LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation biases"
 where: Table 5, p.10.
6. Score ranking differs from value ranking.
 number: the best config delivers $110K-$165K of labour value, the worst $70K-$105K. Codex+Opus (53.45, $86K-$129K) beats Claude Code+Gemini 3 Pro (50.78, $89K-$133K) on score but not on value.
 setup: value is the sum over domains of score times expert-calibrated domain cost. The 94 tasks total 2,420 professional hours, $154K-$231K. SE (946 h) and F&I (803 h) dominate.
 quote: "Codex + Opus 4.6 (avg. 53.45, $86K–$129K) outscores Claude Code + Gemini 3 Pro (avg. 50.78) but delivers less economic value ($89K–$133K)"
 where: p.9, App G.
7. Practitioner gap (survey).
 number: 63.0% low confidence that a model update is better; 25.9% have no explicit eval criteria; 70.4% treat testing as a developer side task; 11.1% have structured test sets with automated pipelines.
 setup: 27 of 50 startup-accelerator companies (54% response), Dec 2025 to Jan 2026.
 quote: "63% of companies report low confidence in whether model updates actually improve their products, 25.9% have no explicit evaluation criteria, and 70.4% rely on developers performing testing as a side task."
 where: Intro, p.2; App J, p.25-26.
8. Production failure modes.
 - Infeasibility: "When a procurement problem has no feasible solution (conflicting constraints), the majority of agent responses fabricate a 'best effort' solution rather than declaring infeasibility". No count given.
 - Cross-section inconsistency: a TAM of $50B in one section and $80B two pages later.
 - Retrieval failure split (Technology Research): "factual hallucination (∼30%), imprecise retrieval (∼35%), rigid search strategies (∼15%), attribution confusion (∼10%), and positive-information bias (∼10%)". Based on "∼130 agent×model evaluation results"; the labelling method is not stated.
 - Quantifiable-criteria tasks score "2–3× higher" than holistic ones.
 - Appendix H.2.6: mapping errors "∼5%" with <20 data points vs "∼25%" with >100 data points.
 - Appendix H.2.4: "26% average cost overruns" from optimizing attributes independently.
 where: Sec 5.4, p.10-11; App H, p.20-24.
9. Construction method.
 - About 1 month of engagement per company, with weekly meetings, and 3-4 refinement cycles per company.
 - Tasks packaged as query.md, task.yaml, files/, .eval/rubric.py (+ ground_truth.json).
 - Every task uses at least 2 grader types, average 2.8 (P&O 3.8, HR 2.0).
 - Scores are s in [0,1], a weighted sum of paradigm results with expert weights; domain scores are unweighted task means; overall is the unweighted mean of 6 domains.
 - Partners raised their quality bars mid-study ("criteria drift").
 - Cost: Claude Code + Opus averages 46 turns and 14 minutes per task.
 where: Sec 3-4, App B, F.

LIMITS
Stated:
- Only 6 domains from 7 companies; no legal, education or creative.
- A single snapshot in time.
- Economic value rests on benefit-multiplier and wage assumptions.
- Only 4 scaffolds.
- 14 of 24 possible pairings tested.
- Sensitivity: the value band widens 61% at the 10th-90th wage percentile. Expert calibration cut the AI hours estimate by 25% (3,240 to 2,420 h).
Unstated:
- Single run for 13 of 14 configs, so differences of 1-4 points (Cursor 61.85, Copilot 61.31, Claude Code 64.41) are within the best config's 3-run noise.
- Judge model equals the top-scoring model (Opus 4.6). Self-preference is only acknowledged, not tested. No judge-swap.
- Meta-eval covers only 20 tasks and 5 unnamed configs.
- Closed-source scaffold versions differ (Codex 0.80.0 vs 0.111.0), so the scaffold effect is confounded with version and model-API compatibility.
- Tasks are proprietary and anonymized, and rubric weights are expert-set, so the benchmark cannot be independently audited. The repository is open but partner data may not be.
- Many Table 3 cells are 11-23 tasks.
- Value is hours-weighted, so SE and F&I dominate.
- Failure percentages come from ~130 results with no stated labelling protocol or inter-annotator check.
- Partners' rubrics were validated with "frontier agents internally", so task difficulty is partly tuned to the tested models.
- No scaffold-only ablation holds the model fixed beyond Opus (and GPT-5.2 across 2 scaffolds).
Dated: model and scaffold versions are as of Mar-Apr 2026.

INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES
- Table 4 "Std" equals the 95% CI half-width in every row: overall std 1.83 and CI 64.41 ± 1.83; HR std 2.14 and CI [33.77, 38.05]. With n=3 a t-based CI would be about 2.5 times wider (t=4.30/sqrt(3)). Either the column is mislabelled or the CI is mean ± 1 std. The "narrow confidence intervals" claim is overstated.
- Figure 3 says "15 Configs × 94 tasks"; the text and Table 3 say 14.
- Appendix G says H&LS hours went 86 to 132 (factor 1.54), but Table 10 shows 154 hours for H&LS. F&I has three different correction factors (0.50, 1.04, 1.00) with no task split. P&O CNY range 49.1-49.7 is nearly degenerate, versus USD 20.4-30.6.
- Survey "15 questions" but items are numbered Q1-Q16.
- Copilot+Opus and Cursor+Opus have identical P&O (88.09) and H&LS (44.06) scores. This is plausible with binary scoring but unexplained.
- The "~130 results" in App H compares to 14 x 94 = 1,316 runs; the subset is not defined.
- "Scaffold matters as much as model" is supported by one clean case (Opus). The GPT-5.2 spread also spans different configs.
- The text calls the 0.69-0.78 kappas "substantial". Expert A vs B (0.691) is the lowest pair, so the judge is not worse than the humans, which is the stronger point.

BUILDS ON: SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., 2024), WebArena (Zhou et al., 2024), OSWorld (Xie et al., 2024) as the foil; Wang et al. (2026) mapping 43 benchmarks to O*NET; Pan et al. (2025) on agents in production; LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023); Agent-as-a-Judge (Zhuge et al., 2024); Panickssery et al. (2024) on self-preference; Yang et al. (2026) for the benefit-multiplier method; O*NET (U.S. Dept of Labor, 2025); BLS wage data; xbench (2025) and AgentIF-OneDay (2026) as the nearest product-evaluation work.

CODE: No code listings. The task package layout is the useful artifact:
"Task Specification (query.md) ... Task Configuration (task.yaml) ... Input Files (files/) ... Evaluation Specification (.eval/rubric.py)" (Sec 3, p.6).
Score formula (App B): s_task = sum_k w_k * e_k(a,t), with sum of w_k = 1.

FIGURES
- Fig 3 (p.5): four-stage requirement-to-benchmark pipeline. The best candidate if a diagram is wanted.
- Fig 2 (p.3): taxonomy of grader paradigms, so a learner sees the mix of graders per task.
- Table 3 (p.9): the model x scaffold x domain grid. This is the better teaching artifact: one table that shows scaffold, domain and ranking flips.
- Fig 1 (p.2) is an overview collage; the extraction is poor.
- Suggested figure: a grouped bar chart of Opus 4.6 across 4 scaffolds (64.41 / 61.85 / 61.31 / 53.45), caveated "single run each, Codex version differs."

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Extraction is clean but equations are mangled (App B) and the Table 1 check-marks are hard to read. The large outputs were truncated by the tool, so I re-read the text in slices from /tmp/alpha.txt. I did not view the PDF images, so figure content is taken from captions only. Appendix H Mode D/E text and the H.2.1-2.2 beginning I read only partly (they went through truncated output).
